title: Chapter XLVII

teacherSummary.text: The Gardiners and Elizabeth return to Longbourn. Mrs. Bennet is hysterical; Mr. Bennet goes to London to search. Lydia's careless letter to Mrs. Forster shows she thinks it a joke.

vocabulary.context: I always thought they were very unfit to have the charge of her; but I was overruled, as I always am.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overrule”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: She was of great use and comfort to us all, and lady Lucas has been very kind; she walked here on Wednesday morning to condole with us, and offered her services, or any of her daughters, if they could be of use to us.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “condole”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + dol (Latin dolere, "to grieve"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: One who rides and guides the first pair of horses of a coach or post chaise
vocabulary.context: “He meant, I believe,” replied Jane, “to go to Epsom, the place where they last changed horses, see the postilions, and try if anything could be made out from them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “postilion”: pos (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Since the ——shire were first quartered in Meryton, nothing but love, flirtation, and officers, have been in her head.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “flirtation”: -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Winding, creeping, or flowing in, quietly or stealthily
vocabulary.context: That he is as false and deceitful, as he is insinuating.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “insinuating”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Jane ran to her uncle and aunt, and welcomed and thanked them both, with alternate smiles and tears.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “alternate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To turn to the advantage of
vocabulary.context: In the afternoon, the two elder Miss Bennets were able to be for half an hour by themselves; and Elizabeth instantly availed herself of the opportunity of making many enquiries, which Jane was equally eager to satisfy.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “avail”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: His temptation is not adequate to the risk.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “adequate”: ad- (Latin ad, "to, toward") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To free from accusation, or the imputation of fault or blame
vocabulary.context: Pray make my excuses to Pratt, for not keeping my engagement, and dancing with him tonight.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “excuse”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Causing to shake or tremble, as by a blow
vocabulary.context: “It does seem, and it is most shocking indeed,” replied Elizabeth, with tears in her eyes, “that a sister’s sense of decency and virtue in such a point should admit of doubt.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “shocking”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Lydia's reputation affected her sisters' marriage prospects too.

significance: Lydia's thoughtlessness exposes the results of indulgence and neglect.
discussionQuestions: What does Lydia's letter reveal about her?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with pride and self-knowledge?

What is Lydia's attitude in her letter?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XLVII,” how does Austen show family in crisis? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLVII develops the idea of family in crisis. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XLVII to complicate the reader's understanding of family in crisis. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLVII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of family in crisis responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLVII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of family in crisis. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: “He meant, I believe,” replied Jane, “to go to Epsom, the place where they last changed horses, see the postilions, and try if anything could be made out from them.
satQuestions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “postilions” most nearly mean?
options: Causing to shake or tremble, as by a blow
One who rides and guides the first pair of horses of a coach or post chaise
To free from accusation, or the imputation of fault or blame

satQuestions.passage: “I have been thinking it over again, Elizabeth,” said her uncle, as they drove from the town; “and really, upon serious consideration, I am much more inclined than I was to judge as your eldest sister does of the matter. It appears to me so very unlikely that any young man should form such a design against a girl who is by no means unprotected or friendless, and who was actually staying in his colonel’s family, that I am strongly inclined to hope the best. Could he expect that her friends would not step forward? Could he expect to be noticed again by the regiment, after such an affront to Colonel Forster? His temptation is not adequate to the risk.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XLVII”?

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: “I have been thinking it over again, Elizabeth,” said her uncle, as they drove from the town; “and really, upon serious consideration, I am much more inclined than I was to judge as your eldest sister does of the matter. It appears to me so very unlikely that any young man should form such a design against a girl who is by no means unprotected or friendless, and who was actually staying in his colonel’s family, that I am strongly inclined to hope the best. Could he expect that her friends would not step forward? Could he expect to be noticed again by the regiment, after such an affront to Colonel Forster? His temptation is not adequate to the risk.”

annotationFocus.label: Theme
annotationFocus.lookFor: statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood
annotationFocus.lookFor: word choices that reveal the narrator's attitude or the scene's feeling

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does Lydia's letter reveal about her? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are overruled, condole, postilions, flirtation, insinuating. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “I always thought they were very unfit to have the charge of her; but I was overruled, as I always am.” Webster's says: To rule over. Now the word history: “overrule”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “condole”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + dol (Latin dolere, "to grieve"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “postilion”: pos (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Lydia's reputation affected her sisters' marriage prospects too. Why does this chapter matter? Lydia's thoughtlessness exposes the results of indulgence and neglect. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to family in crisis.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “I have been thinking it over again, Elizabeth,” said her uncle, as they drove from the town; “and really, upon serious consideration, I am much more inclined than I was to judge as your eldest sister does of the matter. It appears to me so very unlikely that any young man should form such a design against a girl who is by no means unprotected or friendless, and who was actually staying in his colonel’s family, that I am strongly inclined to hope the best. Could he expect that her friends would not step forward? Could he expect to be noticed again by the regiment, after such an affront to Colonel Forster? His temptation is not adequate to the risk.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XLVII,” how does Austen show family in crisis? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about family in crisis, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes family in crisis. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
